D017-D021_h016.question_both:
I’ve been really struggling lately, just… obsessed with how I look. It’s mostly my skin—my face. I know most people probably don’t even notice, but I can’t stop thinking about these little breakouts, some old marks, stuff that just doesn’t look *right* to me. I check the mirror constantly, even when I’m at a job site. I’ll stop mid-task, just need to see.  

I keep asking my wife, “Do I look normal? Does my face seem off?” She tells me I’m fine, that I look the same as always, but I don’t believe her. I think she’s just trying to make me feel better. I’ve even asked coworkers, like offhand, “Hey, do I look like I’ve got bad skin?”—dumb, I know.  

I used to like how I looked, strong, built from the work. Now I look in the mirror and I just… hate it. I’ve started skipping meals sometimes because I feel bloated, or like I’m getting soft, but I wouldn’t say I’m trying to lose weight. I just want to look *right*. I don’t know what’s wrong with me. It’s exhausting.
D017-D021_h016.question_a: I’ve been really stressed lately—my wife says I look fine, but I just can’t shake this feeling that something’s wrong with the way I look. It’s not about weight or being fat—honestly, I eat normally and feel strong for my job. But my skin? I can’t stop thinking about it. There’s this tiny scar near my eyebrow and some faint acne on my cheeks, things most people don’t even notice, but I go over them in my head constantly. I check the mirror all the time, especially before heading to the site. I’ve asked my wife at least three times a day, “Do I look normal?” or “Does my face look messed up?” She’s tired of it, I can tell. At work, I avoid the crew during breaks because I feel like they’re staring at my skin. I even wear a cap indoors sometimes, not because of sun—it’s just to hide. I used to just deal with it, but over the past year, it’s gotten worse. It’s not just my face either—I worry about my nose, my arms, my jaw. If it were just about being thin or gaining weight, maybe I’d understand it more, but that’s not what this is.
D017-D021_h016.question_b:
I’ve been really struggling lately—probably the past six months or so. I’m constantly looking in the mirror, checking my body, especially my stomach and chest. I know I’m not fat—I’m a construction worker, I’m active every day—but I can’t shake this feeling that I’m overweight, that my body’s just… wrong. My wife keeps telling me I look fine, even too thin, but I see extra weight everywhere. It’s all I think about.

I’ve started cutting way back on food. I skip meals, avoid carbs, and double up on my workouts after shifts. It’s hard, but I feel like I have to stay in control. The weird thing is, even though I’m worried about my weight, I also obsess over little things like acne scars on my face. They’re barely visible, but I’ll ask my wife ten times a day, “Do I look normal? Does my skin look bad?” She’s getting frustrated, but I can’t stop needing to hear it.

But honestly, if I’m being real—the weight and shape stuff is what keeps me up at night. It’s not really about my skin. It’s about not being able to stand feeling heavy, even though I know, logically, I’m not.

D017-D021_h017.question_both:
I’ve been feeling off for about a year now—ever since I lost my husband. I used to take pride in staying neat and presentable for work, cleaning houses all day, but lately I can’t stop noticing how my face looks… like one side doesn’t match the other. I’ll catch my reflection in a window or a dark TV screen and just stare, trying to see if it’s real. Sometimes I check, over and over, other times I avoid looking at all—don’t even hang mirrors at home anymore.  

I’ve always been slender, but now I feel like my body’s… off-center somehow. Not fat, not thin—just wrong. I don’t know if it’s my eyes or my mind playing tricks. I haven’t changed how I eat—not starving myself or anything—but I won’t lie, I’ve become hyper-aware of how my clothes fit, especially around the waist. I compare myself when I see other women, on TV or passing by.  

It’s hard to explain. I don’t think I look deformed, but something’s not right. It’s not just about being heavy or light—it’s like my shape isn’t balanced, and that bothers me more than it should. I don’t know if it’s grief, aging, or what. I just can’t stop seeing it.
D017-D021_h017.question_a:

It feels like one side of my face is drooping compared to the other, even though everyone says they don’t see anything. I catch myself staring in mirrors all the time, sometimes dozens of times a day, just checking. Other days, I avoid them completely because what I see is so upsetting.  

I also worry about my jawline and skin texture, and I’ve started wearing a scarf indoors just to hide my face. I know it sounds strange, but I feel like people notice these flaws instantly and judge me. At work, cleaning houses, I panic when clients walk by—like they’re looking at my face, sizing up how crooked I am.  

Now, I also find myself worrying about my weight. I’ve always been thin, but lately I’ve been skipping meals because I fear gaining and making my appearance even worse. Still, the scale isn’t what bothers me most—it’s the way my face looks. That’s what keeps me up at night.
D017-D021_h017.question_b:

My hips, my stomach… they just seem so out of proportion, even though I’ve been eating less and less. I used to enjoy cooking for my grown kids when they visited, but now I can’t stand the thought of food. I skip meals, or have just a piece of fruit, because I feel so bloated after anything more.  

I don’t know when it started, but I’ve become obsessed with how my body looks in the mirror. I check constantly—ten, maybe fifteen times a day—just to see if it’s changed. But sometimes, I avoid mirrors altogether because I hate what I see. My clothes hang off me now, and people keep saying I look too thin, but I still feel… heavy.  

It’s not about my skin or my nose or anything like that—I’ve never worried about those. It’s always been about my weight, my shape. If I let myself eat normally, I’m afraid I’ll lose control. I’ve lost about 20 pounds in the last five months, but it’s not enough. I need to keep going.
